Artificial Intelligence Predicts Hip Fracture Outcomes but Lacks Formal Economic Evaluation

Artificial intelligence and machine learning models developed for hip fracture care consistently forecast the clinical drivers of episode costs but have almost entirely failed to evaluate actual monetary expenses or economic value, according to a scoping review of 236 studies published between 2018 and 2025. Across eight years of peer-reviewed literature, researchers identified an extensive body of work optimizing predictive algorithms for surgical complications, prolonged hospital stays, and post-acute discharge destinations. However, despite the substantial financial burden associated with managing hip fractures in older adults, formal health-economic evaluations measuring cost-effectiveness or budget impact remain entirely absent from the analyzed artificial intelligence literature.

Hip fractures represent some of the most expensive and resource-intensive acute health events encountered in geriatric medicine. Under modern reimbursement models, such as episode-based payment programs and case-mix funding structures, hospitals and healthcare systems absorb considerable financial risks when patient care is complicated by extended lengths of stay, hospital-acquired complications, or specialized post-acute institutional placements. While machine learning algorithms have increasingly demonstrated proficiency in forecasting which patients are most vulnerable to these costly clinical events, health services researchers sought to establish whether the academic literature had successfully connected algorithmic risk stratification to real-world costs, reimbursement mechanisms, or rigorous health technology assessments.

To investigate the extent and characteristics of economic evidence across the field, the research team conducted a comprehensive scoping review adhering strictly to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The investigators designed a structured Boolean search combining thirteen distinct anatomical hip terms with forty-six machine learning and artificial intelligence descriptors. The primary query was executed within the OpenAlex database on July 23, 2026, and was paired with a parallel search in PubMed reconciled at the record level. At peer-review revision, the authors supplemented their methodology with an expanded variant-term search and a known-item recall benchmark tested against two previously published systematic reviews. Eligible sources were restricted to English-language journal articles or reviews published from 2018 through 2025 that implemented an explicitly named computational intelligence method within hip fracture clinical pathways.

Screening and data extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers who systematically categorized eligible investigations. The literature search initially retrieved 432 candidate records from OpenAlex, yielding 230 eligible publications. Three additional eligible studies were identified through PubMed reconciliation, two were recovered via the supplementary query, and one was retrieved from the known-item recall benchmark, culminating in a total analytic sample of 236 peer-reviewed papers. To evaluate economic depth, the reviewers established an investigator-defined six-level classification ladder. The uppermost rung of this evaluative ladder corresponded to the standardized formal methodology codified in the CHEERS 2022 reporting guidelines, while three distinct analytical lexicons were applied to verify that charting thresholds did not accidentally obscure health-economic concepts.

Clinical classification revealed that research activity has concentrated heavily on upfront acute care and prognostic scoring. Diagnostic imaging, automated fracture detection, and procedural guidance systems constituted the largest single focus, accounting for 92 publications, or 39.0 percent of the reviewed literature. Clinical outcome forecasting and healthcare resource prediction formed the second dominant concentration, representing 87 articles, or 36.9 percent of the total volume. Despite this strong methodological focus on estimating patient risks and trajectory markers, explicit economic considerations remained extremely rare across titles and abstracts. Only 16 studies, representing 6.8 percent of the analyzed records, incorporated any explicit references to financial costs or hospital payment mechanisms.

The scarcity of economic assessment became even more pronounced under deeper methodological scrutiny. Across the 236 abstracted investigations, exactly one study, representing 0.4 percent of the sample, constructed an explicit quantitative model simulating monetary expenditure alongside a specific healthcare payment scenario. Not a single paper in the reviewed abstract cohort presented a formal health-economic evaluation. Expanding the screening parameter to its broadest thematic lexicon surfaced only six additional context-only mentions, none of which delivered an economic appraisal. Furthermore, when the researchers audited all 135 openly accessible full-text manuscripts, comprising 57.2 percent of the dataset, they identified zero cost-effectiveness analyses, cost-utility calculations, budget-impact models, or formal health technology assessments.

This absence of economic scrutiny did not stem from an overall shortage of economic methodology within hip fracture scholarship or an unfamiliarity with reporting guidelines among artificial intelligence researchers. The identical search strategy identified 11 formal economic evaluations published during the same period that investigated hip fracture clinical pathways without employing machine learning techniques. In addition, 17 artificial intelligence publications explicitly cited the TRIPOD predictive model reporting standard, confirming that authors adhered to specialized algorithmic reporting frameworks even as none cited the CHEERS health-economic guidelines. The authors concluded that while predictive algorithms reliably detect the primary drivers of episode-based expenses, health economics remains an urgent, unaddressed necessity before these digital tools achieve clinical deployment.

Subject of Research: Health-economic evidence in artificial intelligence research for hip fracture care

Article Title: Health-economic evidence in artificial intelligence research for hip fracture care: a scoping review of 236 studies, 2018–2025

Article References: Shu, X., Li, X., Wang, C., & Peng, X. (2026). Health-economic evidence in artificial intelligence research for hip fracture care: a scoping review of 236 studies, 2018–2025. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-16255-7

Keywords: artificial intelligence, machine learning, hip fracture care, health economics, scoping review, economic evaluation, cost-effectiveness, budget-impact analysis, health services research, PRISMA-ScR, OpenAlex, PubMed, CHEERS 2022, TRIPOD, episode-based payment, case-mix payment, clinical outcome prediction, imaging diagnosis
